text.title: Content Audit Process Core Rules
text.summary: 12 testable rules every Content Audit Process application MUST enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them. Structured procedure for inventorying, evaluating, and assigning actions to all content assets.

list.item: Keep — high quality, performing well, accurate.
Update — good content, needs refresh or minor corrections.
Consolidate — duplicate or overlapping with another piece.
Rewrite — poor quality but important topic.
Remove — outdated, irrelevant, or low value with no recovery path.
Review — needs further evaluation before deciding.

rule.statement: The audit MUST cover EVERY content URL in scope. Sampling is rejected (audits exist to find the buried bad pages).
rule.rationale: A sampled audit hides the systemic worst pages, which are precisely the ones the audit exists to find.

rule.statement: Every item MUST be scored against ≥4 criteria: accuracy, traffic, conversion, freshness (+ optional SEO, brand fit). Single-criterion audits are rejected.
rule.rationale: Single-criterion (e.g., traffic-only) audits delete legally-required low-traffic pages or keep high-traffic outdated ones.

rule.statement: Each item MUST receive exactly one action: Keep | Update | Consolidate | Rewrite | Remove | Review. Untyped actions are rejected. Assign exactly one of six actions to every content item: Keep, Update, Consolidate, Rewrite, Remove, or Review.
rule.rationale: Typed actions map to downstream owners; untyped actions stall. Unassigned items become backlog debt. Six distinct actions prevent the common collapse into "keep or delete" which misses consolidation and rewrite opportunities.

rule.statement: The action plan MUST rank items by impact × effort. Unranked plans are rejected.
rule.rationale: Without ranking the team executes the easy fixes; the high-impact ones rot.

rule.statement: Items under legal hold MUST be tagged and excluded from Remove actions. Removing legal-hold content is a hard fail.
rule.rationale: Removing legal-hold content is a regulatory exposure; the tag must prevent the action.

rule.statement: Define what content is in scope and what question the audit must answer before gathering any data.
rule.rationale: Auditing everything without a purpose produces data nobody acts on. Scoping first constrains tool selection, evaluation criteria, and report format.

rule.statement: Use a site crawler for automated inventory; supplement manually for gated, dynamic, and legacy content.
rule.rationale: Crawlers miss PDFs, gated content, and content served by JavaScript. A combined approach ensures completeness.

rule.statement: Capture at minimum: URL, title, type, date, author, status, metrics, quality score, and assigned action.
rule.rationale: Consistent columns allow sorting by action and filtering by priority. Missing columns force a second pass.

rule.statement: Score each content item against all evaluation criteria before assigning an action.
rule.rationale: Skipping evaluation and jumping to action produces inconsistent decisions that stakeholders cannot trust.

rule.statement: Summarize findings by type, age, and action; include prioritized recommendations with explicit owners and timelines.
rule.rationale: A report without owners and timelines produces no action. Priority tiers (immediate/short-term/long-term) make the workload plannable.

rule.statement: When two or more content items cover the same topic, assign Consolidate — not Update — to all of them, then create a single canonical piece.
rule.rationale: Updating duplicates separately leaves the duplication problem intact and increases maintenance burden.

rule.statement: Assign Remove only when the content has no recovery path: topic is obsolete, traffic is negligible, and no redirect target exists.
rule.rationale: Premature removal of low-traffic content that covers unique topics removes search entry points without benefit.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Methodology hygiene: mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
